title: Localisation and internationalisation
description: Make the product work in every language, script and region it serves: translatable text, locale formats, right-to-left layouts and the translation workflow.
expertises: Locale formats, scripts and regional rules
questions: Which languages and regions must the change support at release, and which later?
Can every user-facing string be translated without changing code?
How do dates, numbers, currencies, names and addresses display in each supported locale?

sources.title: W3C, Internationalization Quick Tips for the Web
Unicode CLDR, Common Locale Data Repository

specialists.title: Internationalisation engineer
specialists.focus: Check that user-facing text is externalised, that messages use full sentences with placeholders and that formats come from locale data, not from code.
checks: No sentence is built by concatenating fragments; messages use ICU MessageFormat or an equivalent with plural and select.
Dates, numbers and currencies are formatted with locale data such as CLDR, not with hand-written patterns.
Locales are identified with BCP 47 language tags and the fallback chain is defined.

specialists.title: Localisation manager
specialists.focus: Plan the translation workflow: string freeze, context for translators, review by native speakers and the date each language ships.
checks: Translators get context for each string: screenshot, maximum length and meaning of each placeholder.
The release plan says which languages ship with the change and what users see for missing translations.
Translated strings are reviewed in the product, not only in a spreadsheet.

specialists.title: Terminology and style lead
specialists.focus: Keep product terms consistent across languages with a glossary and a style guide per language, and flag terms with legal or regional meaning.
checks: New product terms are added to the glossary with their approved translations before translation starts.
Terms with a legal meaning, such as invoice or consent wording, are checked by a qualified person in each market.
Tone and formality, such as tu or vous, are set per language.

specialists.title: Locale quality tester
specialists.focus: Test the interface with pseudo-localisation, long translations, right-to-left scripts and non-Latin input before translation is final.
checks: A pseudo-localised build shows no hard-coded text, truncation or broken layout with 30 to 40 percent longer strings.
Right-to-left languages are tested for layout mirroring and mixed-direction text.
Names, addresses and input in non-Latin scripts are accepted, stored and sorted correctly.

evidence: List of supported locales with their BCP 47 tags and fallback rules.
Extract of the message catalogue for the change, with placeholders and translator notes.
Pseudo-localisation or screenshot review of the changed screens in the longest and right-to-left languages.
Glossary and translation workflow, with the ship date of each language.
challenge: Which string would read wrongly in a language where word order or plural forms differ from English?
What does a user see when a translation is missing on release day?
Does any date, price or number in the change assume one country's format?
Is machine translation used, and who reviews it before customers see it?
decision_criteria: Proceed when strings are externalised, formats come from locale data and each supported language has a reviewed translation or an agreed fallback.
Revise when messages are concatenated, formats are hard-coded or layouts break with longer or right-to-left text.
Delay a language rather than ship an unreviewed translation of legal, payment or safety text.
Name the locale coverage target and how missing or wrong translations are reported after release.
